beats.narration_text: Hola, this is Liam, in for Bear. Today we take apart Tin Knockout, Tharun Maheswararao's Godot slice for assignment two: a tin wind-up diver toy boxing his repainted twin in a goldfish bowl, after the toy shop closes. The prompt on screen is an illustrative reconstruction, not a saved transcript.

beats.role_note: walker B01 — what was built and what this film explains. Hesitant writer; the correction is the misconception the body dismantles (sound does not drive the fight).
beats.narration_text: Tin Knockout is one round of toy boxing where every move costs wind. The fight drives the sounds, never the other way round. So this film reads a few lines of code, then shows you what each one does on screen.

where every move costs wind.
Sound decides the fight.

beats.role_note: Concept and the four pillars, plainly, over a real engine frame.
beats.narration_text: The concept, plainly. You are Bolt, a tin wind-up deep-sea-diver toy. Rivet is the same toy, repainted copper and verdigris. The spring in your back is your stamina. Every punch, cutlass swing and cork pop-gun shot unwinds it, and so does walking. Hold S to rewind: one ratchet click per quarter turn, ten wind each, but rewinding locks you in place. Run down to zero and the toy stalls, empty. Get hit while rewinding or empty, and you are knocked down. Four pillars: every move costs wind, tin you can hear, read the fight at a glance, and toys after closing.

beats.role_note: One asset traced design → prompt → raw → edits → in-engine: CHAR-JAB.
beats.narration_text: One asset, traced end to end: the jab. It starts as a spec: pose P04 on a pose sheet Claude drew in code, and panel three of the storyboard. That pose became a flat init sketch. SDXL-Turbo, image to image, at strength zero point six, eight steps, seed forty-three, turned it into this raw five twelve square output, from the prompt on screen. The first pose batch drifted off-model, the failure predicted as F1, so it was rejected and redone against one reference image, which Tharun picked from four finalists. Then an edit script removed the background with rembg, painted two eyes on the helmet glass, and scaled him to three hundred thirty-six pixels, feet at two forty, four thirty-five. Rivet is the same file, recoloured. And in the engine, the jab lands.

beats.role_note: Cause → effect, the cause: sprite.centered = false in fighter.gd.
beats.narration_text: Here is the cause and effect. In fighter dot g d, line seventy-two creates the sprite, and line seventy-three sets centered to false. Every pose is drawn on a four eighty by four fifty canvas with the feet at two forty, four thirty-five, and line two sixty-seven already offsets the sprite by minus those feet. Leave it centred, and the art is shifted twice.

props.title: The Sprite Anchor Fix
props.source: Godot editor reconstruction · godot/fighter/fighter.gd lines 71–74 at 64c037a, verbatim
props.code:
func _ready() -> void:
	sprite = Sprite2D.new()
	sprite.centered = false   # offset = -FEET puts the feet on the node origin (was double-shifted when centred)
	add_child(sprite)

beats.role_note: Spring mechanism: _rewind turns the key, adds wind per quarter turn, emits rewind_tick.
beats.narration_text: Now the spring. This function runs while S is held. Line two oh eight turns the key three hundred and sixty degrees a second. Every ninety degrees, line two eleven adds ten wind, and line two thirteen emits rewind tick: one ratchet click per quarter turn. Line two oh seven stops the clicks once the spring is full. Nothing here plays a sound. It only announces the click.

props.title: Rewinding the Spring
props.source: Godot editor reconstruction · godot/fighter/fighter.gd lines 206–214 at 64c037a, verbatim
props.code:
if wind >= MAX_WIND:
		return                  # full: the key stops turning, no more clicks
	crank_deg += CRANK_DEG_PER_S * dt
	while crank_deg >= 90.0 and wind < MAX_WIND:
		crank_deg -= 90.0
		wind = minf(MAX_WIND, wind + WIND_PER_CLICK)
		wind_changed.emit(self, wind)
		rewind_tick.emit(self)
	key_spin = crank_deg

beats.role_note: Sound wiring: sfx.gd listens to gameplay signals.
beats.narration_text: Here is how sound is wired. In s f x dot g d, watch connects to the fighter's signals. Line thirty-one: hit landed plays the jab or cutlass sound, pitched lower when blocked. Line thirty-two: projectile fired plays the pop. Line thirty-three: each rewind tick plays one ratchet click. Lines thirty-four to thirty-six: entering EMPTY plays the stall. Gameplay never calls this node.

props.title: Sound Listens, Gameplay Decides
props.source: Godot editor reconstruction · godot/audio/sfx.gd lines 30–36 at 64c037a, verbatim
props.code:
func watch(f: Fighter) -> void:
	f.hit_landed.connect(func(_a, attack, blocked): play(attack if attack != "pop" else "jab", 0.8 if blocked else 1.0))
	f.projectile_fired.connect(func(_f): play("pop"))
	f.rewind_tick.connect(func(_f): play("rewind", 1.0 + 0.04 * (_f.wind / 100.0)))
	f.state_changed.connect(func(_f, _old, new_state):
		if new_state == Fighter.S.EMPTY:
			play("empty"))

beats.role_note: Result of B11: the recorded test output from an isolated copy, plus the seam check.
beats.narration_text: Here is the real output, from a fresh run on an isolated copy. Twenty-five checks, zero failed, and the muted and unmuted end states match number for number. The first ever run had eight failures. The cause was the test's own setup order: Rivet fired a cork before the test froze him. The setup was fixed, a one and a half second pop-gun cooldown was added at round start, and no expected value changed. The music loop seam check passes too. The engine's exit warnings are shown as printed.

beats.role_note: VERDICT — tested vs uncertain; models per asset; revision shown.
beats.narration_text: The verdict, at revision six four c zero three a. Tested: twenty-five automated checks pass, the music loop seam passes, and a muted run ends in exactly the same state as an unmuted one. Tharun's own playtest, sound on and then muted, is recorded in TEST-REPORT dot m d. He found the music fine on its own and the muted slice still readable, but the game and the characters very simple, and the mix full of metal sounds. On checking, that came from the dense tin effects, the rewind clicks and clangs, not the music. Uncertain: Claude picked those sound effects by signal analysis, because Tharun asked it to choose, and Claude cannot hear. The bowl is seen from outside, though the concept says inside. Rivet is a pattern, not an AI. The eyes are hand-painted on every pose, and the win pose uses a different seed. This 4K take also differs from the headless dry run, because physics stepping changes under fixed f p s. Models: all art is SDXL-Turbo, under Stability's non-commercial research licence. The six sound effects are AudioLDM 2, C C BY N C S A. The waltz is MusicGen small, C C BY N C. All ran locally on an Apple M4.

beats.role_note: YOUR TURN — a useful Walker prompt read aloud, one bounded change + prediction, credits, revision; Liam signs off before the locked outro.
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here is a useful Walker prompt. Please use Walker to change rivet brain dot g d so a cornered Rivet blocks instead of rewinding when Bolt is closer than one hundred seventy pixels, add one test for it, and state your prediction before you run it. Mine: Rivet gets knocked down while rewinding less often, and rounds last longer. Write yours down first, then run the tests. Tharun's own next step is just as bounded: a quieter rewind click and a lower effects mix, then richer character art. Toward the full game, add a real opponent AI and weapon pickups from the toy box. Credits, plainly. Tharun chose the game and the weapons, rejected reusing his assignment one character, picked Bolt, picked the reference image from four finalists, and approved the documents. Claude Code wrote the prompts, code, tests and edit scripts, picked the poses by the character sheet's rules, and picked the sounds by signal analysis. This voice is Kokoro text to speech. The source shown is revision six four c zero three a. Liam, in for Bear.
